title: Shinran and other power
hookLine: Shinran: awakening comes through Amida's power, not our own effort
carry: other power: even the trust is given

lines: A MONK COMES DOWN THE MOUNTAIN.
NO OTHER PRACTICE WAS WITHIN REACH.
cards: A monk comes down a mountain.

Tradition says Shinran spent long years training on Mount Hiei, the monastery mountain above Kyoto, with study, chanting and long nights of practice, and came down convinced that none of it had changed what was wrong inside him.
In the city he found Honen, the teacher of the nembutsu, and stayed.

A disciple wrote down what Shinran said about that choice: even if Honen had misled him, and saying the name led him to hell, he would have no regret, because no other practice had ever been within his reach.

teach.h: JIRIKI, SELF POWER. TARIKI, OTHER POWER.
teach.b: First, two words, building on the Shinran you met in year three. Jiriki means self power: awakening built by your own effort, your discipline, your merit.
Tariki means other power: the power of Amida's vow, working on you from outside your own effort. Yesterday the easy path was Tanluan's boat. Tariki is the boat.
Second, what Shinran did with it. For him, other power reaches all the way down.
Not only is the Pure Land Amida's gift; even the trust that receives it, even the nembutsu on your lips, is Amida at work, not a technique you perform well. Third, the line people stop at.

teach.h: HOW MUCH MORE AN EVIL PERSON.
teach.b: The same record of his words, the Tannisho, has him say: even a good person is born in the Pure Land, so how much more an evil person.

The record's explanation: the person who trusts their own goodness still leans, a little, on self power. The one who knows they have nothing to offer leans entirely on the vow. Fourth, what it is not.

teach.h: NOT AN EXCUSE; NOT A METHOD.
teach.b: Other power is no excuse to stop caring how you live; the record has Shinran warning against people who did wrong on purpose, thinking the vow would cover it. And Pure Land teachers differ here.
In Honen's Jodo school, the nembutsu is practiced often and earnestly, as the practice the vow chose.
In Shinran's Jodo Shinshu, the emphasis falls on receiving, not achieving. Both say the name; they place the effort differently. What Shinran found coming down the mountain was not a better method.
It was the end of needing one.

how: In Jodo Shinshu, Shin Buddhists understand birth in the Pure Land as the work of Amida's vow, other power, rather than their own effort; they say the nembutsu, and hear Shinran's teaching in temple talks and in readings from the Tannisho.

o: train harder: more fasting, more nights awake.
come down the mountain and follow Honen and the nembutsu.

practice: Settle into the chair and notice what is already holding you up: the seat, the floor, the ground under the building, and let your weight go into it. Notice the breath, which keeps going whether you manage it or not.
For the rest of the sit, stop helping: let the chair hold you, and let the breath breathe.

wordCard.voice: Tariki. Other power: in Shin Buddhism, the power of Amida's vow, which does what self power cannot. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese: tariki, other power, set against jiriki (自力), self power.

carryVoice: Your line: other power: even the trust is given. That's tariki, Amida's vow doing what effort can't. Rest well, and come back tomorrow.
